title: Six Months In: The Iran War’s Global Impact | BloombergNEF
gist: Six months after the Feb 2026 US/Israel-Iran conflict disrupted Strait of Hormuz flows, BNEF's regional analysts find energy security has become the primary driver of clean-energy policy worldwide: import-exposed nations with domestic resources (China, India, Indonesia) were cushioned, oil/LNG-import-dependent nations (Japan, Korea, Europe, most of Africa) were hit hardest, and EV/solar demand has surged broadly except in the US, where subsidy expiry and policy has blunted the transition response.

themes.theme: India & Southeast Asia: Subsidy Politics and EV Surge

insights.claim: India and Indonesia derive roughly two-thirds of their electricity from domestic coal, which largely insulated their power sectors from the Iran war's fuel price shock, while Vietnam and the Philippines' heavy reliance on imported fuels was exposed, prompting both to roll out fuel subsidies, tax exemptions, and power-market interventions.
insights.speaker: iterhorst
insights.so_what: Domestic coal/resource endowment is now a visible determinant of macro resilience to Hormuz-linked shocks; countries lacking it (Vietnam, Philippines) are turning to subsidies that strain public finances.
insights.locator: India and Indonesia produce about two-thirds of their electricity

insights.claim: In the Philippines and Malaysia, rooftop solar additions surged as consumers responded to the Iran war's fuel and power price shocks.
insights.speaker: iterhorst
insights.so_what: A geopolitically-driven energy-security shock is functioning as an unplanned demand catalyst for distributed solar in Southeast Asia.
insights.locator: In the Philippines and Malaysia, rooftop solar additions surged

insights.claim: Monthly EV sales in Indonesia and the Philippines are now roughly double what they were a year earlier, and India's passenger EV sales passed 30,000 units in June and July 2026 (up from under 20,000/month a year earlier), after India lifted gasoline-price-suppression measures in May and Indonesia, the Philippines, and Vietnam all rolled out new EV-promotion policies.
insights.speaker: iterhorst
insights.so_what: Transport-sector fuel exposure, not power-sector exposure, is the primary channel through which the war is accelerating EV adoption across South/Southeast Asia — a trackable, quantifiable EV demand tailwind.
insights.locator: Consumers are responding: monthly electric vehicle sales

themes.theme: China: Energy Security Reinforces the Transition

insights.claim: China's pre-war build-out of energy security — one of the world's largest petroleum reserves plus record domestic gas production — cushioned it from the Gulf conflict shock and let it act as a balancing force in global oil markets by cutting its own imports.
insights.speaker: iterhorst
insights.so_what: China's strategic reserve and domestic-supply strategy, built ahead of the crisis, is now paying off as resilience versus peers — a template other import-dependent economies may emulate.
insights.locator: By placing energy security at the heart of national policymaking

insights.claim: In China, energy transition and energy security are proving mutually reinforcing rather than competing priorities, with rapidly scaling renewables joining domestic coal plants to make power generation more self-reliant.
insights.speaker: iterhorst
insights.so_what: This is a core framework claim: in China's case, decarbonization and energy-security policy are aligned, not in tension — a contrast to the US and parts of Europe covered elsewhere in the piece.
insights.quote: Overall, the energy transition and energy security are proving to be mutually reinforcing rather than competing priorities in China.
insights.locator: Overall, the energy transition and energy security

insights.claim: More than half of new cars sold in China are now electric, causing gasoline demand to sink, while renewables deployment is beginning to plateau as key policy reforms take effect, following a period that pushed installed capacity to a very high level.
insights.speaker: iterhorst
insights.so_what: Crossing the 50% EV-of-new-sales threshold in China marks a structural, not cyclical, decline in domestic gasoline demand with direct implications for refiners and oil demand forecasts.
insights.locator: Gasoline demand is sinking as more than half

insights.claim: China, the world's largest producer of clean-energy equipment (solar modules, EVs, batteries), has logged five straight months of record exports of these products measured in dollar terms since the war began, a surge that started with a domestic export-subsidy change but has persisted.
insights.speaker: iterhorst
insights.so_what: A five-month streak of record clean-tech exports post-war signals China is capturing global market share as other regions turn to Chinese solar/EV/battery equipment to hedge fuel-price shocks — relevant for competitive positioning of non-Chinese clean-tech manufacturers.
insights.locator: Exports of these products surged in the month immediately after the war began

themes.theme: Africa & Middle East: Oil Exposure Drives Solar and Resilience Plans

insights.claim: Major African economies — Morocco, Egypt, Nigeria, Ghana, and South Africa — were net importers of refined oil products before the war and have directly suffered from the resulting fuel price shocks, with impacts compounded because most African homes and businesses rely on unreliable grids backed by petrol/diesel generators.
insights.speaker: iterhorst
insights.so_what: Generator-dependence turns a global fuel-price shock directly into a domestic power-cost shock across much of Africa, an amplification channel not present in grid-reliable economies.
insights.locator: African nations have been hurt by their strong dependence

insights.claim: Africa's imports of Chinese solar equipment grew 37% from 1H 2025 to 1H 2026, the highest growth of any region globally over that period, with the boom now spanning the continent (South Africa, Nigeria, DR Congo, Egypt, Morocco) rather than being concentrated in single countries as in prior cycles.
insights.speaker: iterhorst
insights.so_what: A continent-wide, not country-specific, solar boom implies a more durable and broad-based structural demand shift for Chinese solar exporters and African distributed-energy players.
insights.quote: Africa’s imports of Chinese solar equipment grew 37% from 1H 2025 to 1H 2026, the highest rise in any region globally over that period.
insights.locator: The silver lining has been the availability of inexpensive solar equipment

insights.claim: Middle East oil producers' economic exposure to the war correlates directly with their capacity to bypass the Strait of Hormuz: Saudi Arabia and the UAE leaned on existing bypass infrastructure and will invest further in redundancy, while Oman has emerged a relative 'winner' due to direct ocean access; the war has also raised regional debt costs, hurting near-term clean-power project economics even as it may seed a longer-term renewables growth phase (freeing domestic fossil fuels for export).
insights.speaker: iterhorst
insights.so_what: Hormuz-bypass infrastructure is becoming a differentiator of Gulf-producer resilience, and higher debt costs are a near-term headwind for Gulf renewables financing even as the long-term security case for renewables (to free up fossil fuels for export) strengthens.
insights.locator: The war’s economic impact on Middle Eastern oil producers

insights.claim: Almost half of the EU's jet fuel imports and nearly a fifth of its diesel imports pass through the Strait of Hormuz, but the impact on jet fuel supply has been milder than expected due to relatively low demand, alternative import sources, and higher domestic refinery output.
insights.speaker: iterhorst
insights.so_what: Europe's refined-product exposure to Hormuz was a widely feared vulnerability that has so far under-delivered on the downside, a useful base-rate check against worst-case Hormuz disruption scenarios.
insights.quote: Almost half of the European Union’s jet fuel imports and nearly a fifth of its diesel imports pass through the Strait.
insights.locator: Europe has been heavily exposed to the Iran war

insights.claim: Renewables now supply 35% of power across Europe's five core power markets, up from 24% in 2021, leaving Europe's power system better placed to absorb this gas-price shock than it was during Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
insights.speaker: iterhorst
insights.so_what: An 11-point renewables-share gain since 2021 is now functioning as measurable energy-security insurance for European power markets during a second major geopolitical gas shock.
insights.quote: Renewables now supply 35% of power across the five core European power markets, up from 24% in 2021.
insights.locator: Europe’s electricity system is also better placed

insights.claim: European policy responses have mostly focused on shielding consumers from higher costs rather than accelerating the energy transition, which weakens incentives to cut fossil fuel demand and strains public finances; Germany is an exception, raising onshore wind auction volumes by 12 gigawatts in response to the war, and BNEF expects other European markets to at least maintain, if not raise, renewables ambition.
insights.speaker: iterhorst
insights.so_what: Consumer-shielding policy is a near-term drag on Europe's decarbonization pace even as the security rationale for renewables strengthens — Germany's 12GW onshore wind auction increase is a concrete, trackable signal of the alternative path.
insights.locator: Policy responses have so far focused on shielding consumers

insights.claim: Europe heads into winter with gas storage at a decade low and a tight middle-distillate market, and may take a lesson from China by building larger strategic fuel reserves to cushion future shocks.
insights.speaker: iterhorst
insights.so_what: Decade-low gas storage heading into winter is a concrete near-term risk marker for European gas/power prices this heating season.
insights.locator: Europe may also take a lesson from China

themes.theme: Latin America: Commodity and EV Windfall

insights.claim: Oil producers already ramping up output — Brazil, Argentina, and Guyana — posted record revenues as prices spiked and importers sought non-Gulf suppliers, while higher copper and lithium prices benefited Chile and Peru, and rising oil prices pushed Brazil (already the world's second-largest biofuel producer) to raise its mandated ethanol blend share in gasoline.
insights.speaker: iterhorst
insights.so_what: Latin American commodity exporters (oil, copper, lithium) and biofuel producers are direct beneficiaries of the war's price effects, a regional relative-value angle for commodity-linked equities.
insights.locator: On the oil side, markets that were already ramping up production

insights.claim: Brazil's monthly battery-electric vehicle sales passed 15,000 units for the first time in April 2026 and surpassed 25,000 by July 2026, while Brazilian imports of Chinese BEVs and plug-in hybrids reached about 166,000 units combined in April-May 2026 — the two biggest months on record for such imports — against 401,000 total vehicles of any drivetrain sold in Brazil over the same period.
insights.speaker: iterhorst
insights.so_what: Chinese EV imports made up a strikingly large share (roughly 40%) of all Brazilian vehicle sales in April-May 2026, underscoring how fast Chinese automakers are penetrating Latin America amid the fuel-price shock.
insights.quote: Some 166,000 BEVs and plug-in hybrids were imported in April and May, making these the two biggest months for such imports on record.
insights.locator: Moreover, since the war began, Brazilian imports

insights.claim: The analyst expects Latin America's EV sales boost could decelerate if oil prices moderate and ethanol supply increases, but sees the region's mining-sector boost as more durable, since electrification is structurally increasing demand for transition metals and ongoing supply constraints should keep benefiting resource-rich Latin American nations.
insights.speaker: iterhorst
insights.so_what: A differentiated forecast: treat the Latin American EV-sales surge as a war-linked, potentially transient effect, but treat the region's mining/transition-metals tailwind as structural and durable.
insights.locator: If oil prices moderate and ethanol supply increases

insights.claim: The US economy has proven largely resilient to the war so far, as ample domestic natural gas production and maxed-out LNG export terminal capacity kept domestic gas and power prices in check, blunting any sense of urgency among consumers, businesses, and most policymakers to move away from fossil fuels.
insights.speaker: iterhorst
insights.so_what: US energy-transition momentum is effectively decoupled from this geopolitical shock because domestic gas abundance is absorbing the impact — a contrast to Japan/Korea/Europe where the shock is a policy catalyst.
insights.locator: The US economy has proven largely resilient

insights.claim: Higher gasoline prices boosted US demand for conventional hybrids and used EVs, but with federal EV purchase subsidies now gone, US consumers have not flocked to new EVs, and US automakers are not reversing their Trump-administration-era pivot toward large ICE pickups and away from EVs.
insights.speaker: iterhorst
insights.so_what: The removal of federal EV subsidies appears to be structurally capping new-EV demand response in the US even amid a fuel-price shock — a key divergence from EV surges seen in Asia and Latin America.
insights.locator: Higher gasoline (petrol) prices have boosted demand

insights.claim: Since the war began, Germany and South Korea have committed to buy more Canadian fuel and invest in Canadian fuel-production infrastructure, as Canadian PM Mark Carney pursues an 'energy superpower' agenda combining oil exports, trade deals, expanded clean power and EV production, more carbon capture, and higher carbon prices in oil-producing Alberta — a strategy the article frames as internally conflicted between energy-security/economic goals and continued decarbonization.
insights.speaker: iterhorst
insights.so_what: Canada is simultaneously scaling fossil-fuel exports and clean-energy investment, a dual-track strategy investors should track for internal contradictions (e.g., Alberta carbon pricing vs. expanded oil/gas exports) rather than assuming a clean-energy-only trajectory.
insights.locator: Since the war began, Germany and South Korea

themes.theme: Japan & South Korea: Import Dependence Reframes the Transition

insights.claim: Before the war, about 70% of South Korea's and 90% of Japan's crude oil supplies passed through the Strait of Hormuz; after the conflict began, regional LNG spot prices soared, forcing both nations to tap strategic petroleum reserves, increase coal-fired generation, and buy expensive spot LNG cargoes to maintain reliable power.
insights.speaker: iterhorst
insights.so_what: These are among the most Hormuz-exposed major economies in the world (70-90% of crude supply), making them a bellwether for how import-dependent Asia responds to the conflict.
insights.quote: Pre-war, 70% of Korea’s and 90% of Japan’s crude oil supplies passed through the Strait of Hormuz.
insights.locator: As highly import-dependent energy economies

insights.claim: In April 2026, South Korea explicitly cited the Iran war in a new plan to reach 100 gigawatts of renewables and more than 20% renewable power generation by 2030, alongside investment in grids, storage, electrification, and faster EV adoption framed as energy security.
insights.speaker: iterhorst
insights.so_what: A concrete, dated policy commitment (100GW renewables, >20% generation share by 2030) explicitly triggered by the war gives investors a trackable South Korean renewables target tied to a specific catalyst.
insights.locator: Korea made that link explicit in April

insights.claim: Japan has made less of a policy pivot than Korea, but the crisis reinforced the energy-security logic behind nuclear restarts and domestic renewables already embedded in its 2040 strategy, even as Tokyo remains wary of trading over-reliance on Gulf oil/gas for over-reliance on Chinese-made clean energy goods; both governments are cushioning fossil-fuel prices today while arguing locally produced electricity is tomorrow's answer, and six months in, the war has made energy security a stronger case for decarbonization than climate policy alone.
insights.speaker: iterhorst
insights.so_what: Japan's explicit wariness of Chinese clean-tech dependence is a structural constraint on its solar/EV supply chain choices, likely favoring domestic or non-Chinese suppliers even as it accelerates nuclear and renewables.
insights.quote: Six months in, the war has not visibly transformed project pipelines, but it has made energy security a stronger case for decarbonization in Japan and Korea than climate policy alone.
insights.locator: The contradiction is that both governments

themes.theme: Australia: Fuel Price Shock Meets Early EV Policy

insights.claim: Abundant domestic natural gas production and LNG exporters willing to forgo maximum export pricing kept Australia's domestic gas prices low, holding power prices at or even below pre-war levels, while Australia's dependence on imported refined oil caused soaring pump prices and localized diesel scarcity from panic buying, especially in rural areas.
insights.speaker: iterhorst
insights.so_what: Australia shows a split exposure profile — power-sector insulation via domestic gas but transport-sector vulnerability via imported refined products — a useful template for assessing other gas-rich, oil-import-dependent economies.
insights.locator: A combination of abundant natural gas production

insights.claim: Nearly as many EVs were sold in Australia in the first half of 2026 as across all of 2025, as the country's first EV policy began to bite just as petrol and diesel prices spiked.
insights.speaker: iterhorst
insights.so_what: The coincidence of new EV policy support and a fuel-price spike appears to have produced an outsized, front-loaded EV sales jump in Australia worth watching for durability once support rolls off.
insights.locator: Nearly as many EVs were sold in the first half of 2026

insights.claim: As initial EV policy support rolls off and the conflict drags on, BNEF flags concerns about Australia's ability to reliably source low-cost oil cargoes, warning the country could face sticky inflation given how heavily exposed its transport, agriculture, and resource sectors remain to international oil prices.
insights.speaker: iterhorst
insights.so_what: A specific macro risk flag: Australia's inflation trajectory is tied to oil-price exposure across three key sectors, a factor for rate and currency views if the conflict persists.
insights.locator: Despite this, as initial policy support rolls off
